Learning Objectives
Describe the pathophysiology of head trauma and the distinction between primary and
secondary brain injuries.
Explain the effects of decreased cerebral perfusion pressure with regard to adverse outcomes.
Identify serum biomarkers for the diagnostic workup and outcome prediction in patients with
traumatic brain injury.
Outline the risk of hypoxia and hypotension with regard to secondary brain injury.
Review the concepts of appropriate resuscitation for limiting the risk of secondary brain injury.
Recognize patients who require early neurosurgical consultation, hospital admission, or
transfer to a higher level of care.
Define the optimal timing and modality of long bone fracture fixation in polytrauma patients
with associated head injuries.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Background
The key aspect for understanding the pathophysiology of traumatic brain injury (TBI) relates
to the notion that the extent of neurologic injury is not determined by the extent of the initial
traumatic impact itself but evolves over time.
The evolution of secondary brain injury is characterized by a complex cascade of molecular
and biochemical reactions to the initial trauma. These events trigger an acute inflammatory
response within the injured brain, leading to adverse outcomes after TBI.
Evidence of secondary brain injury has been found on autopsy in 70% to 90% of individuals
with fatal head injury.
The intracranial activation of the complement cascade mediates breakdown of blood-brain
barrier function and subsequent leakage of neurotoxic molecules from the peripheral blood
stream into the subarachnoid space.
The extent of secondary brain injury is characterized by neuroinflammation,
ischemia/reperfusion injuries, cerebral edema, intracranial hemorrhage, and intracranial
hypertension.
Despite recent advances in basic and clinical research and improved neurointensive care for
TBI patients, no pharmacologic agent is available to mitigate or prevent the evolution of
secondary brain injuries.
Iatrogenic factors, such as permissive hypotension, prophylactic hyperventilation,
overzealous volume resuscitation, and inappropriate timing and technique of associated
fracture fixation, contribute to worsening of secondary brain injury.
Hypotension and hypoxemia during the early resuscitation of patients with multiple injuries
represent the lethal duo and are the most important predictive factors of adverse outcomes
after TBI.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
TBI represents the leading cause of death in trauma patients, ranking higher than
mortality related to exsanguinating traumatic-hemorrhagic shock.1-4 The main root
cause of the high mortality rate is attributed to secondary cerebral insults because of
hypoxia and hypotension, intracranial bleeding, and cerebral edema resulting from the

complex underlying neuroinflammatory pathophysiology of secondary brain injury5,6
(Figure 1).
Figure 1 Algorithm shows the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury.
(Courtesy of Philip F. Stahel, MD, FACS, Denver, CO.)
Overview
Most individuals with TBI typically suffer a mild cerebral concussion. This corresponds with a
diffuse brain injury with preserved consciousness.
The classic cerebral concussion results in a reversible loss of consciousness, a certain degree
of a memory loss (amnesia), and reversible neurologic dysfunction.
Fatal intracranial hemorrhage will occur in approximately 3% to 10% of all individuals with mild
TBI (cerebral concussion).


Overview
Focal brain injury patterns are induced via direct concussion/compression forces or
penetrating trauma mechanisms. Conversely, diffuse brain injury results from indirect
trauma mechanisms, such as sudden deceleration or rotational acceleration. The most
severe form of TBI is represented by so-called diffuse axonal injury or by focal
contusions with bleeding inside or around the brain.7,8
Epidemiology
TBI represents the leading cause of death and disability in individuals younger than 40 years in
industrialized countries.
In the United States alone, approximately 1.5 to 1.8 million people sustain a head injury each
year, of which approximately 500,000 require hospital admission.
The annual economic burden of direct and indirect costs from TBI is estimated to be
approximately $50 billion in the United States.
The clinical outcomes of patients with severe TBI remain poor, with a high mortality rate of
approximately 35% to 40%.
Anatomy
The cranial anatomy encompasses the scalp, skull, meninges, brain, and ventricular system.
The scalp represents the soft-tissue envelope around the skull and is characterized by
extensive blood supply. Uncontrolled blood loss from scalp lacerations may lead to life-
threatening hemorrhagic shock.
The skull provides a protective cavity for the brain (cranium or neurocranium) and the
structure for the face. The cranium is divided into a roof (calvarium) and a base.
The calvarium comprises the frontal, occipital, and parietal bones, which are connected
through fibrous sutures. The cranial base consists of six bones and provides the articulation
with the cervical spine, facial bones, and mandible.
The meninges consist of three layers that cover the brain: the dura mater, arachnoid mater,
and pia mater. Meningeal arteries in the epidural space between dura and skull are prone to
traumatic rupture, which may lead to life-threatening epidural hematomas. The subdural
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:35 AM
AAOS | Traumatic Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004015
4/28

space lies between the dura and arachnoid mater. Bridging veins from the brain surface to the
venous sinuses may tear from shearing injuries and lead to subdural hematomas.
Subarachnoid hemorrhage occurs in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) space between the
arachnoid mater and the pia mater, which is the third meningeal layer that is firmly attached
to the brain surface.
The brain is comprised of the cerebrum, brain stem, and cerebellum. The cerebrum consists of
two hemispheres that are separated by the falx cerebri. The brain stem consists of the
midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata. The cerebellum lies in the posterior fossa and
connects to the brain stem and spinal cord.
The ventricular system is filled with CSF, which is continuously produced and absorbed by the
choroid plexuses. The presence of hemorrhage in the CSF is a sign of severe TBI and adverse
outcomes.
Injury Classification
The classification of TBI is determined by injury severity using the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) or
by morphology using CT without contrast.
A patient’s level of consciousness is evaluated using the GCS score (Table 1), which grades the
severity of TBI as mild (GCS score, 13 to 15), moderate (GCS score, 9 to 12), and severe (GCS
score, 3 to 8).
The GCS is one of the most commonly used clinical classification scales worldwide.
The historic GCS grading scale from the 1970s was recently modified to be more easily
applicable and to account for non-testable parameters.

morphologic severity of TBI. Hereby, intracranial lesions are classified as focal injuries,

surgically evacuated versus non-evacuated hematomas, and grade I through IV diffuse injuries
(Figure 2).
Figure 2 Table shows the Marshall classification of head CT scans. (Reproduced with permission
from Marshall LF, Marshall SB, Klauber MR, et al: The diagnosis of head injury requires a


Injury Classification
A post-resuscitation GCS score is necessary to grade the severity of TBI and account for
the confounding variable of cerebral hypoperfusion in patients with traumatic-
hemorrhagic shock.8,9 Of the three underlying criteria (eye opening, verbal response,
motor response), the best motor response represents the most reliable predictor of
outcomes. The GCS must be re-evaluated and documented at regular time intervals to
detect a deterioration in GCS score over time (beware of patients who talk and die).8 The
morphologic TBI classification is determined via a CT scan of the head without
contrast.10 This includes the descriptive assessment for a skull fracture, open fracture
with intracranial air, intracranial hematomas (ICHs), diffuse axonal injury, cerebral
contusions, and cerebral swelling with midline shift.
SEND FEEDBACK

Associated Injuries
In patients with TBI, spinal injuries represent the most frequent associated injury pattern that
requires an elevated level of suspicion during the initial diagnostic workup.
Substantial associated injuries, such as blunt chest trauma, intra-abdominal hemorrhage,
pelvic ring disruptions, and long bone fractures, must receive adequate attention because of
their potential for contributing to secondary brain damage.
Inconsiderate timing and modality of long bone fracture stabilization in polytrauma patients
with TBI increases the risk of preventable cerebral insults and secondary brain injury.
Co-management of TBI and Long Bone Fractures
Patients with a TBI and associated long bone fractures, as classically exemplified by femoral
shaft fractures, represent a highly vulnerable patient population because of the risk of
sustaining preventable second hit injury.
The conundrum related to defining the optimal timing and modality of long bone fracture
fixation in patients with associated head injuries remains a subject of ongoing debate.

Co-management of TBI and Long Bone Fractures
Early definitive femoral shaft fracture stabilization was advocated by Bone et al11 in a
historic landmark article from 1989; however, polytrauma patients with TBI may be
highly vulnerable during early definitive fracture fixation because of hemodynamic
instability, refractory hypoxemia, or intracranial hypertension.12 Experimental animal
studies demonstrated that femoral reaming and nailing leads to intracranial pressure
(ICP) levels higher than 15 mm Hg in models of hemorrhagic shock/resuscitation with or
without associated TBI.13,14 These data are corroborated by clinical studies that
analyzed changes in ICP and cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) in patients with severe
TBI who underwent reamed intramedullary nail fixation of associated femur fractures.15-
17 Multiple studies have demonstrated that early definitive femoral fracture fixation
(within 24 hours) is associated with early episodes of hypoxia and hypotension and
adverse neurologic outcomes in patients with TBI.17-20 To avoid the adverse effects of
early total care (ETC) on the vulnerable brain, the concept of damage control
orthopaedics (DCO) has been advocated by applying a staged approach that involves
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:35 AM
AAOS | Traumatic Brain Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004015
8/28

initial temporary external fixation and delayed definitive fixation of femoral shaft
fractures; this is a preferred neuroprotective modality for polytrauma patients with
TBI21-23 (Figure 3). Compared with ETC, the DCO approach with delayed conversion to
definitive management has been shown to decrease the initial surgical time and
intraoperative blood loss without increasing the risk of procedure-related complications,
such as infection and non-union. The subsequent procedure after DCO-related
intramedullary reaming and nailing of femoral shaft fractures should be performed
outside of the neuroinflammatory priming window, after the post-injury
hyperinflammatory response has subsided, ideally within 2 weeks of the initial
procedure.24 The delayed conversion procedure is considered safe after ICP has
normalized and patients are awake, oriented, and fully resuscitated.18,25,26
Figure 3 Image shows management strategies for femoral shaft fractures in polytrauma
patients with a traumatic brain injury. DCO = damage control orthopaedics, ETC = early
total care. (Courtesy of Philip F. Stahel, MD, FACS, Denver, CO.)

Decision-Making Strategy for TBI With Associated Femoral Shaft
Fracture
DCO via spanning external fixation in all patients with severe TBI (GCS score ?8, intracranial
pathology on CT scan, including cerebral edema, midline shift, subdural/epidural bleeding, or
open head injuries)
Optional DCO in all patients with moderate TBI (GCS score, 9 to 13) or patients with a GCS
score of 14 or 15 with minor intracranial pathology observed on CT scans (eg, traumatic
subarachnoid hemorrhage that warrants observation only); concomitant neurosurgical
procedures may be performed at the same time as DCO (eg, emergency craniotomy).
No additional surgical procedures (second hit) in patients with refractory intracranial
hypertension or unexplained deterioration in neurologic examination
Conversion from external to internal fixation in patients with TBI who recovered from a
comatose state and are awake and alert (GCS score, 13 to 15) or comatose patients with a
stable ICP (<20 mm Hg) and CPP in a normal range (>80 mm Hg) for more than 48 hours
ETC for long bone fractures in all patients with mild TBI (GCS score, 13 to 15) and normal initial
craniocerebral CT scans
Temporary skeletal traction as a valid adjunct for patients in extremis (ie, in severe protracted
traumatic-hemorrhagic shock and coagulopathy, who cannot be taken to the operating room
until adequately resuscitated)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
The initial assessment of polytrauma patients with associated TBI is performed via a
standardized approach according to Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol.
A brief history is obtained using the AMPLE mnemonic: allergies, medications, past
illnesses/pregnancy, last meal, and events/environment related to the mechanism of injury
Detailed knowledge of the exact mechanism of injury will enhance understanding of the
patient’s injury severity and risk of deterioration.
The patient history pertinent to TBI must include loss of consciousness and
antegrade/retrograde amnesia.
SEND FEEDBACK


Patient History and Physical Examination
A TBI is suspected based on the history of a trauma mechanism related to indirect high-
energy acceleration/deceleration injuries (fall from a height; motor vehicle
collision/motorcycle collision, passenger ejection; presence of associated cervical spine
injury) and direct trauma to the head, including penetrating injuries.27 After ensuring
vital functions with a patent airway, adequate oxygenation, and stable hemodynamics, a
rapid neurologic examination is performed as part “D” (Disability) of the ABCDEs). This
includes assessment of the GCS as a brief objective method of determining the level of
consciousness and evaluation of pupil size, symmetry, and reaction.8 Clinical signs of
basilar skull fractures include leakage of CSF from the ear (otorrhea) or nose
(rhinorrhea), periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes), and retroauricular ecchymosis
(Battle sign). Rarely, skull fractures may be associated with neurologic dysfunction of the
cranial nerves VII (facial paralysis) and VIII (hearing loss) or with a carotid artery
dissection. Open skull fractures expose the cerebral surface and are associated with a
high risk of infections (meningitis, meningoencephalitis).8
Imaging Studies
CT of the head without contrast is the preferred initial imaging modality for evaluation of TBI.
Screening plain radiographs of the skull for the detection of fractures represent a historically
antiquated diagnostic modality and are considered obsolete.
MRI rarely is indicated in the early diagnostic workup for patients with acute TBI. Indications
for MRI include assessment of diffuse axonal injury in comatose patients with normal CT
findings and workup for the differential diagnosis of a cerebrovascular stroke.
Computed Tomography
CT without contrast is considered the preferred modality for the early imaging evaluation of
patients with TBI.
Indications
All patients with moderate or severe TBI (GCS score <13)

Patients with mild TBI (GCS score, 13 to 15) and any of the following variables:
GCS score <15 for more than 2 hours
Loss of consciousness for longer than 5 minutes
Amnesia before impact for longer than 30 minutes
High-energy trauma mechanism of injury
Clinically suspected skull fracture
Clinical signs of basilar skull fracture (hemotympanum, otorrhea/rhinorrhea, Battle sign,
raccoon eyes)
Pupil asymmetry
Peripheral neurologic impairment
Anticoagulation
Severe headache
Intoxication
Confusion and strange behavior
Nausea and vomiting
Age older than 65 years
Interpretation of Findings
Skull fractures in younger patients generally are a sign of high-energy trauma. Fractures occur
in the cranial vault or in the base of the skull. The presence of a linear vault fracture alone is
associated with a 400-fold increased risk of an ICH (Figure 4).

Figure 4 Axial CT scans of the head of a 40-year-old man who was assaulted with a baseball bat.
A, CT scan shows a segmental, comminuted fracture of the left temporal and parietal bone
(arrows) with associated subdural hematoma. The small air bubbles under the skull fracture
indicate an open fracture. B, CT scan without contrast shows an underlying subdural hematoma.
(Courtesy of Philip F. Stahel, MD, FACS, Denver, CO.)
Intracranial lesions are stratified as diffuse or focal injuries. By definition, diffuse brain injuries
present as normal on CT scans. Mild diffuse brain injury is a simple concussion, whereas
diffuse axonal injury represents a neuronal shearing injury from high-energy acceleration-
deceleration mechanisms and is associated with a dismal prognosis (Figure 5).

Figure 5 Axial CT scans of the head of a 43-year-old man who sustained a high-speed
multivehicle deceleration injury. At the scene of the injury, the patient was comatose, with a
Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3, and was intubated. A, Initial CT scan without contrast shows
diffuse brain swelling with effacement of the intracranial subarachnoid spaces. The arrow
indicates the residual lateral ventricle in the left hemisphere. B, CT scan without contrast
obtained 3 days postinjury shows a small, punctuate subarachnoid hemorrhage. Despite
maximum intensive care therapy, the patient died from uncontrolled cerebral edema with
tonsillar herniation. (Courtesy of Philip F. Stahel, MD, FACS, Denver, CO.)
Focal lesions include epidural, subdural, and intracerebral hematomas, as well as cerebral
contusions.
Epidural hematomas are uncommon but dangerous because they are underestimated (so-
called lucid interval), with the potential for rapid deterioration and adverse patient outcomes.
These hematomas present in a biconvex or lenticular shape on axial CT scans and result from
a tear to the middle meningeal artery (Figure 6). Conversely, subdural hematomas are of
venous origin because of shearing injuries to bridging veins of the cerebral cortex.

Subdural hematomas are more common and are observed in approximately 30% of all
patients with a severe head injury. In contrast to the lenticular shape of epidural bleeding, the
shape of subdural hematomas conforms to the contour of the brain (Figure 7). Subdural
hematomas are surrogate markers of severe underlying parenchymal brain injury.

Cerebral contusions and intracerebral hematomas are common injury patterns detected in
approximately 30% of all patients with severe TBI. Most contusions are observed in the frontal
and temporal lobes (Figure 8). Contusions can evolve over time and form intracerebral
hematomas with perifocal neuroinflammation and cerebral edema, which may lead to a mass
effect requiring surgical decompression.

Management
The treatment of most patients with mild or moderate TBI is nonsurgical.
The management of severe TBI follows the standardized evidence-based guidelines published
by the Brain Trauma Foundation.28
Patients with severe TBI (GCS score ≤8) require immediate endotracheal intubation for airway
protection and adequate ventilation and oxygenation.
Prophylactic hyperventilation (pCO2 <25 mm Hg) is considered obsolete and not
recommended because of the risk of preventable cerebral insults.
The concept of permissive hypotension should not be advocated in polytrauma patients with
associated TBI because of the potential detrimental effect on preventable secondary cerebral
insults.
Elevated ICP values (>20 mm Hg) are associated with adverse outcomes after TBI. Indication
for the placement of indwelling ICP devices for continuous ICP monitoring should be

considered under the following circumstances:
Severe TBI (GCS score ≤8) with abnormal admission CT scan
Severe TBI (GCS score ≤8) with normal CT scan and prolonged coma (>6 hours)
Postoperative monitoring after surgical hematoma evacuation
Neurologic deterioration (GCS score ≤8) in patients with initially mild or moderate TBI
Patients with a head injury who require prolonged mechanical ventilation (eg, for
management of associated extracranial injuries), unless initial CT scans are normal.

Management
The main goal in the early treatment of patients with TBI is the prevention and
restoration of variables that contribute to the evolution of secondary brain injury,
including hypoxemia, hypotension, hypercarbia, and hypoglycemia.20 Patients with a
severe TBI (GCS ≤8) require immediate endotracheal intubation for airway protection
and adequate ventilation and oxygenation.8 The preferred fluid replacement therapy for
patients with a TBI consists of isotonic electrolyte solutions, such as Ringer lactate.24
Urinary output helps guide patient response to resuscitation, with a goal of more than
0.5 mL/kg/hr in adults and 1 to 2 mL/kg/hr in pediatric patients.24
Because of the interrelation between CPP with ICP and mean arterial pressure (MAP), an
increased systemic blood pressure should not be therapeutically lowered in patients
with a head injury because this may be reflective of demand hypertension to retain
adequate cerebral blood flow (CPP = MAP − ICP).7 Similarly, permissive hypotension
should not be advocated in polytrauma patients with am associated TBI because of the
potential detrimental effect on preventable secondary cerebral insults.19 According to
the Monro-Kellie doctrine, the total intracranial volume remains constant, implying that
expanding mass lesions will result in reduced CPP.8 Therefore, CPP maintenance above
70 to 80 mm Hg may have to be therapeutically achieved via surgical evacuation of
intracranial mass lesions and via attenuation of brain swelling with the use of osmotic
drugs (eg, mannitol) and therapeutic CSF drainage via intraventricular catheters.26

Intensive Care Unit Management
Intensive care unit management of polytrauma patients with associated head injuries primarily
focuses on preventing secondary brain injury by maintaining adequate oxygen delivery and
hemodynamic stability. This includes the prevention of hypoxemia, hypercarbia, and
hypotension, with a goal of PaO2 higher than 13 kPa, PaCO2 between 3.3 and 4.5 kPa, and MAP
greater or equal to 80 mm Hg.
The historic concept of blind prophylactic hyperventilation has been largely abandoned
because of the inherent risk of inducing focal ischemic insults.
Additional aspects of the baseline intensive care of TBI patients includes the prevention of
hyperthermia, hyperglycemia, and hyponatremia.26,28,29
Pharmacologic Therapy
Currently, no effective pharmacologic therapy is available to prevent or attenuate the
evolution of secondary brain injury after TBI.
Mannitol is used to reduce elevated ICP levels and typically is administered as a 20% bolus (20
g mannitol in 100 mL). Mannitol augments intravascular volume, increases cerebral blood flow,
and diminishes intracranial volume. Classic indications for the application of mannitol include
clinical signs of transtentorial herniation (ie, loss of consciousness, decerebrate rigidity,
ipsilateral pupil dilatation, contralateral hemiparesis) or progressive neurologic deterioration
with decreasing GCS scores. If administering mannitol, serum osmolarity should be kept to less
than 315 mOsm/L, and hypovolemia must be avoided via adequate fluid replacement.
Systemic hypotension is considered a contraindication for mannitol because of the risk of
increasing cerebral ischemia.
Hypertonic saline in concentrations of 3% or higher represents another therapeutic modality
for reducing elevated ICP and may be a preferred treatment option for hypotensive trauma
patients.
Barbiturates are effective in reducing ICP; however, their use is restricted for intensive care
therapy with continuous electroencephalographic monitoring.
Corticosteroids are considered obsolete and contraindicated in the pharmacologic treatment
of patients with TBI.
Surgical Management
Indications
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004015
19/28

Scalp wounds are controlled via surgical débridement and wound closure for early
hemorrhage control and infection prevention.
Depressed skull fractures represent an indication for surgical elevation. The rule of thumb for
surgical management is a depression greater than the thickness of the adjacent skull observed
on CT scans.
Intracranial lesions with a mass effect, midline shift observed on CT scans, elevated ICP (>20
mm Hg), and penetrating brain injuries are general considerations for neurosurgical
management via hematoma evacuation and decompressive craniectomies, as indicated.

Indications
Surgical indications in patients with a TBI include scalp wounds, depressed skull
fractures, intracranial mass lesions, and penetrating brain injuries. Although scalp
wounds can be addressed by a general trauma surgeon, any intracranial lesion must be
managed by a consulting neurosurgeon.8 Approximately one-third of patients with a
severe TBI require emergent surgical treatment for evacuation of mass lesions, most
commonly acute subdural hematomas.7 Even minor lesions in the temporal or posterior
fossa may cause compression to the brain stem and obstruction of CSF flow, which are
indications for early surgical treatment. In patients with a mild or moderate brain injury,
a craniotomy is performed to manage stable hematomas on a less urgent basis.26
The timing of surgical treatment depends on the clinical condition of the patient based
on GCS, neurologic examination, and CT findings.24 Surgical hematoma evacuation
typically is performed via a craniotomy, with the bone flap replaced at the end of the
procedure. If considerable mass effect or swelling of the injured cerebral hemisphere is
present, a decompressive craniectomy is performed, with the bone flap left off at the
end of the procedure. This helps alleviate elevated intracranial pressure and prevents
recurrence of intracranial hematomas.
Considerations for Surgical Evacuation of ICHs

In general, an ICH causing neurologic deterioration or more than 5mm of midline shift on CT
scan should be evacuated as soon as possible.
Evacuation of acute subdural hematomas more than 10 mm thick
Evacuation of acute subdural hematomas of less than 10 mm in comatose patients with severe
parenchymal injuries and mass effect
For epidural hematomas, surgical evacuation generally is indicated, except in clinically stable
patients with a small epidural hematoma and minimal pathologic findings (GCS score, 14 or
15).
Evacuation of large ICHs in patients with focal neurologic deficits and/or a midline shift
observed on CT scans.
Nonsurgical Management
Patients with a GCS score of less than 15 who do not meet the already mentioned criteria for
surgical treatment should be admitted as inpatients for observation under the following
circumstances:
Abnormal CT scan
History of prolonged loss of consciousness
Deteriorating level of consciousness
Persistent focal neurologic impairment
Skull fracture
Open TBI
CSF leak
Moderate to severe headaches
Ethyl alcohol or drug intoxication
No reliable companion at home
Complications
General complications of severe TBI
Any ICH causing neurologic deterioration or more
Cerebral edema may lead to supratentorial swelling and herniation of the brain.
Ischemic brain injury after brain herniation or focal cerebral vasospasms
Posttraumatic immunosuppression, leading to increased susceptibility to pulmonary
infections, sepsis, and multi-organ failure.

Specific treatment-related complications
Cerebral insult from recurring hypoxemia and hypotension, leading to preventable
secondary brain injury
Incomplete surgical evacuation of intracranial mass lesions
Recurrence of intracranial bleeding after surgical hematoma evacuation.
Surgical infections, including meningitis, meningoencephalitis, brain abscess.
Cerebral vasospasms after therapeutic hyperventilation
Prophylaxis: maintain pCO2 in constant range (3.3 to 4.5 kPa) and monitor arterio-jugular
lactate concentrations, jugular bulb oximetry, and frequent transcranial Doppler
sonography
Complications of barbiturate coma: cardiovascular depression, hepatotoxicity,
immunosuppression, and increased incidence of pulmonary infections
Complications of severe TBI are stratified into general complications and specific treatment-
related complications.7 General complications in patients with a critical TBI include neurogenic
pulmonary edema resulting from fluid overload; syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone
secretion, which is characterized by hyponatremia, hypo-osmolarity, and a urinary sodium level
higher than 25 mEq/L; and disseminated intravascular coagulation induced by damaged brain
tissue, which represents a powerful activator of the coagulation cascade.8 Other general
complications include stress ulcers leading to gastrointestinal bleeding; pressure sores from
prolonged bed rest; and heterotopic ossification, which is characterized by bone formation in
tissues that normally do not ossify. The incidence of heterotopic ossification is as high as 80% in
patients with an isolated severe TBI and is a major cause of morbidity and persisting disability in
the later phase of neurorehabilitation.
Outcomes
Prospective data from the Traumatic Coma Data Bank in the 1990s revealed that patients with
severe head injury (GCS score ?8) had an overall mortality rate of 36% at 6 months postinjury.6
An initial GCS score of 3 was associated with the highest mortality (76%), compared with
patients with a GCS score of 6 to 8 (18%).
Patients with moderate head injury (GCS score, 9 to 13) are at particular risk for intracranial
complications, with an overall mortality rate of approximately 7%.

Outcomes
The GCS, although originally not intended as a prognostic index, is a strong indicator of
outcome after closed head injury.8 Although mortality represents a parameter of
outcome that is easy to define, residual impairment in terms of neurologic, cognitive, or
behavioral deficits is more difficult to assess. Numerous tests and scores offer different
approaches for determining posttraumatic neurologic and
neuropsychologicimpairment.30,31 For example, the Disability Rating Scale and the
Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) represent traditional measures of global outcome that
provide a basis for comparing the results of treatment at different centers. If analyzed
using the GOS, only approximately 60% of patients with moderate head injury have an
overall good recovery by 6 months after trauma (GOS score, 5), whereas a moderate
(GOS score, 4) to severe disability (GOS score, 3) is described in 26% and 7% of patients,
respectively. Analysis of outcomes after mild head injury (GCS score, 14 or 15) frequently
revealed posttraumatic neuropsychologic sequelae beyond 3 months.8 Currently, no
reliable serum biomarkers are available to predict long-term outcomes after TBI.32,33
Common Errors of Practice
Delayed resuscitation from hypotension and hypoxemia
Delayed endotracheal intubation in patients with a GCS score of less than or equal to 8.
Inadequate attention to associated injuries (thoracic, abdominal, orthopaedic)
Underestimating mild or moderate head injury, assuming no intracranial pathology is present
(patients who talk and die)
Underestimating comatose patients with normal CT scans (diffuse axonal injury)
Failures in awake patients
Inadequate frequency of neurologic examinations.
Not obtaining a CT scan on neurologic deterioration or change in pupil size/reactivity.

Pearls and Pitfalls
Closed head injury is the leading cause of death in young patients in industrialized countries.
Patients who survive the initial injury are susceptible to secondary cerebral insults, which are
initiated by the release of neurotoxic and inflammatory endogenous mediators.
Hypoxia and hypotension in the early resuscitative period represents the key parameters for
induction of secondary brain injury and adverse outcomes.
The neuroinflammatory response in the injured brain contributes to cerebral edema,
increased ICP, and decreased CPP.
ICP monitoring and CPP therapy are recommended as a standard of care for patients with
severe closed head injury. ICP should be maintained below 15 mm Hg and CPP should be
maintained above 70 mm Hg to avoid secondary insults from cerebral hypoperfusion.
If a CPP 70 mm Hg or higher cannot be achieved by lowering the ICP, the MAP should be
artificially raised via catecholamines (CPP = MAP ? ICP)
Arterial demand hypertension in patients with a head injury should not be lowered
therapeutically because this physiological response is aimed at maintaining an adequate CPP
after cerebrovascular autoregulation has failed.
